signals.title: Red Bull to title sponsor 2026 Australian Motorcycle Grand Prix
signals.summary: The final edition at Phillip Island will see Red Bull take top billing MotoGP is pleased to confirm that Red Bull will serve as title sponsor of the 2026 Australian Motorcycle Grand Prix at Phillip Island. The appointment forms part of Red Bull's broader partnership with MotoGP in Australia, including title sponsorship of the Australian Grand Prix as the championship enters a new era in Adelaide from 2027. The latest agreement reinforces Red Bull's decades-long commitment to motorcycle racing and rider development. Next weekend's event will mark MotoGP's final visit to Phillip Island before the Australian Grand Prix relocates to Adelaide the following year, bringing the curtain down on one of the most iconic chapters in the sport's history. To recognise MotoGP's final race at Phillip Island and Red Bull's first Australian Grand Prix as title sponsor, a range of Red Bull fan experiences and displays will feature across the event, highlighted by a special aerobatic display from Red Bull Air Race World Champion, Matt Hall. As the championship prepares to begin its next chapter in Adelaide, the Red Bull Australian Motorcycle Grand Prix will provide a fitting final celebration of MotoGP at Phillip Island, with fans from across Australia and around the world set to tune in as the championship battle intensifies. Carlos Ezpeleta, Deputy CEO of MotoGP, said: "We're delighted to welcome Red Bull as title sponsor of the 2026 Australian Motorcycle Grand Prix. Their support reflects a long-standing commitment to motorcycle racing and makes them a fitting partner for what will be a significant event for MotoGP in Australia this year and in 2027 and 2028 in Adelaide. "Phillip Island has played an iconic role in the history of the championship and has provided fans with many unforgettable moments over the years. As we prepare for our final visit to the circuit before beginning a new chapter, we're looking forward to celebrating another fantastic Australian Grand Prix with riders, teams and fans from around the world." signals.title: STEVE ENGLISH OPINION: How Pirelli pushed the boundaries in WorldSBK for over 20 years
signals.summary: As the Pirelli era comes to a close, WorldSBK commentator Steve English looks back at a time when the Italian company didn't just supply tyres to WorldSBK; it also helped reshape the series and the racing world. When the chequered flag falls on Sunday in the final race of the 2026 MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship season, an era will come to an end. It will be far more significant than the end of Nicolo Bulega's (Aruba.it Racing – Ducati) reign as Champion. After 22 years and 660 races as the Championship's control-tyre supplier, Pirelli will bow out of WorldSBK. When the Pirelli era started it came on the back of a dominant season from Ducati. In 2003 the Bologna machines won every race of the season and while they are likely to do the same again this year, it is an anomaly. Since then, WorldSBK has continued to provide opportunities for multiple manufacturers to compete at the front. Gone were the days of tyre specials for factory teams or manufacturers being saddled with uncompetitive rubber. Now, the same tyre was available for everyone on the grid, and you needed to work hard to make it work for you. It’s been a remarkable 22 years of partnership between WorldSBK and Pirelli. It hasn’t always been perfect, there have been some mishaps along the way, but when James Toseland crossed the line on February 29 th , 2004, he made history. The Englishman was the first rider to win with a control-tyre in WorldSBK. At the time, introducing a control-tyre was seen by some as a step backwards for a major World Championship. A tyre war had traditionally driven development, with manufacturers and tyre companies pushing each other to find performance. Why remove that competition from racing? Pirelli's answer was to take the development battle in a different direction. They wanted to use WorldSBK to develop tyres that customers could buy and use on their own bikes. It proved to be the recipe for the brand for the next two decades. Despite the scepticism at the start of the control-tyre era almost every major championship in the world has followed suit. Whether it’s MotoGP or Formula 1, cars or bikes, the decision to implement this strategy has now been followed in almost every series. Pirelli wanted to ensure that the development war hadn’t ended but rather that its purpose changed. The goal was to allow customers to buy and use the same tyres used in the series. Pirelli ensured that these are production tyres for production bikes. The goal of Pirelli in WorldSBK was always to follow the old adage of Superbike racing; win on Sunday, sell on Monday. Customers could buy the exact same tyre in a shop and fit them to their bikes. Whether it was the treaded tyres used in WorldSSP or the slicks of WorldSBK, if you were going on a track day you could buy the same tyre used by the WorldSBK stars of the era. It was a remarkable step that surprised many within racing when Pirelli proved their credentials on track and in the showroom. Being the control-tyre offered commercial benefits to Pirelli, but it also benefited WorldSBK. A constant stream of developments saw changes to compounds, profiles and sizes. It changed how racing developed. One lap Superpole tyres were slowly phased out. When WorldSBK introduced the Tissot Superpole Race, Pirelli brought a specific tyre for the 10-lap battle. Lap records have continued to fall and race times have tumbled. Development never stopped. When the Pirelli era draws to a close on Sunday, the company will leave behind more than 22 years of results and records. It will leave a legacy that helped prove a control-tyre could serve the needs of both World Championship racing and the customers who take those same products onto the track. signals.title: PREVIEW: Salvador and Artigas prepare for a decisive final-round WorldSPB showdown at Jerez
signals.summary: It all comes down to this. Two riders separated by 12 points to decide the first-ever WorldSPB title The FIM Sportbike World Championship has put on a show all year in the category’s maiden campaign, and the final round looks set to be no less dramatic, with a shootout for the title. The Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia will once again host the final round of the year, and it will be a home Pirelli Spanish Round for the top two title contenders as a litany of tight battles within the top ten unfold behind them. Current leader David Salvador (Team ProDina Kawasaki XCI) and Xavi Artigas (MTM Kawasaki) are separated by just 12 points with 50 points left to play for; a narrow margin given WorldSPB’s frequent groups of riders fighting for podium positions in the class. In 2025’s dramatic final WorldSSP300 round here at Jerez, he took P2 in Race 1 behind eventual Champion Benat Fernandez (Kove Racing Team 109), and despite fighting for the win in Race 2, a last-lap irresponsible riding penalty applied to him by FIM WorldSBK Stewards sent him back to a P16 finish. Nonetheless, he and teammate Antonio Torres earned the Teams’ title, a feat he will look to repeat in 2026. To clinch the Riders’ title as early as Race 1, Salvador will need to outscore Artigas by at least 14 points; if that doesn’t happen, the title fight will go to a decisive final-race showdown between the pair. Australian rider Carter Thompson (Team BrCorse) has caught fire over the last four rounds, and with a maiden win in the class in Race 2 at Cremona, he now holds third place in the Riders’ Championship standings. Thompson finished both races off the podium last season here in WorldSSP300, which may be a promising omen for the rider in P4 behind him, Torres. The #47 took two podiums here in that same category over the last two seasons, and with such a slim margin separating the two, don’t expect either rider to give an inch. British rider Fenton Seabright (PHR Performance Triumph) missed the podium last time out for the first time in the last four rounds, and a return to the rostrum would help safeguard his fifth-place position in the Championship, with a posse of riders as close behind as just four points. Riding in P6 with the Brit in his sights, Belgian rider Ferre Fleerackers (Track & Trades Wixx Racing) found a way back onto the podium at Cremona for his first silverware since Assen. With little left to lose, he currently rides as the top Suzuki rider. Look for him to try to break his GSX-8R into the top five over the final two races. Matteo Vannucci (Revo-M2) holds P7 just seven points behind the Belgian but hasn’t enjoyed the same recent return to pace. Vannucci started the season with terrific pace on his Aprilia machine; he will fight tooth and nail, free of pressure, to try to get his confidence back in this final round. Like his Suzuki-powered teammate Fleerackers, two-time WorldSSP300 Champion Jeffrey Buis enjoyed a tremendous start to the season, but that momentum has slowed to a crawl as he’s taken a total of five points over the last two rounds. Looking for a high note to end this season on, the Dutchman will throw the kitchen sink at the Spanish circuit. It’s a similar story for Italian Bruno Ieraci (CM Triumph Factory Racing) in ninth place. He’s shown flashes of brilliance on his Triumph machine, including a maiden win at home at Misano, but since then, positives have been few and far between. Holding tenth place, Dutch rider Loris Veneman (MTM Kawasaki) will miss the season’s final round after he crashed out at Turn 3 in Race 2 at Cremona, he will be replaced by Spanish rider Roberto Fernandez who competed in the class at Aragon where he took his first point in Race 1. Hungry to break into the top ten at the 11 th hour, Spanish rider Alvaro Fuertes (Deza-Box 77 Racing Team) arrives home after a high of P4 at Cremona, his best round of the season to put him within four points of the #71. Behind him in P12, British Triumph rider Harrison Dessoy (PHR Performance Triumph) prepares for a final assault on the top ten just two points behind Fuertes; the Englishman has a feather in his cap as he arrives in Andalucia, having taken his second WorldSPB podium in P2 in Race 1 in Italy. Arai Agaska (ProGP NitiRacing) has been declared unfit and will hope to get the all-clear from the medical centre ahead of the round’s action on track. Continuing to fill in for German rider Phillip Tonn, French rider Hugo De Cancellis (Kove Racing Team 109) will compete on the Kove 450RR alongside Benat Fernandez. Riding as the round’s lone wildcard, inaugural WorldSSP300 Champion Marc Garcia (Yamaha MS Racing FIMLA AD78) returns to the paddock to appear in WorldSPB’s first-ever season as well. signals.title: PREVIEW: Herrera arrives to Jerez with one hand on the title, a tall task ahead of Neila seeking an upset
signals.summary: The final round of the WorldWCR season promises an epic battle for the Championship and emotional battles up and down the grid The FIM Women’s Circuit Racing World Championship prepares to send off its 2026 season on a high note as for the third consecutive season, the Championship will be decided in the final round. Maria Herrera (Terra & Vita GRT Yamaha WorldWCR) leads with a large margin behind her ahead of Beatriz Neila (Ampito Crescent Yamaha), and the #6 could crown herself Champion in Race 1. The #36 behind her, however, won’t be pulling any punches, and she will push the title decider to Sunday. In other news, it was announced that the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia and its Pirelli Spanish Round will be the final WorldWCR round featuring Yamaha equipping the class . From 2027 on, Chinese manufacturer CFMOTO will propel the category forward. The calculations in the Championship fight are relatively straightforward this time around. The #6 sits 44 points ahead of Neila with 50 points left on the board; as a result, Herrera will be Champion on Saturday if she can finish among the top ten. Neila, however will need quite a hand from lady luck this weekend, as she will need to win and hope for an error from the #6 to preserve her title hopes. Herrera arrives hot, having collected 45 out of 50 potential points from their most recent round back in July at Donington Park, and she has landed atop the podium twice at Jerez in the past. Her first victory here arrived in 2024 while she fought with Ana Carrasco (Honda Racing World Supersport) for the first-ever WorldWCR title, and the second was taken last season in Race 1 which was a critical step to putting her first World Championship victory on ice. For the #36, Neila was sent sprawling onto the grass at Donington Park after contact with Herrera, but she showed her composure with a Race 2 triumph on Sunday. The Madrid native has taken four podiums here in the past, has not yet stood on the top step at Jerez. Just behind them, an interesting fight has developed for the final step on the podium. Roberta Ponziani (Klint Racing Team) arrives in southern Spain with a single point in hand on her rookie teammate Paola Ramos. The Spanish rookie has won two races so far in her first campaign as a full-time rider after making her debut as a wildcard at Jerez. That round, she took a stunning maiden win; foreshadowing a strong rookie campaign in which her main issue has been struggles with inconsistency and bad luck. Four races have finished with ‘SuperPao’ outside the points, her most recent took the form of a crash out at Donington Park. Similar to the #36, the crash occurred after contact with Herrera, which the #6 was later penalised for. On the other side of the box, Ponziani has been much more consistent. She’s bagged two podiums so far, and has finished every race between third and sixth on the occasions when she has finished the race. A distant shot at third place remains for Muklada Sarapuech (Yamaha AD78 FIMLA by EEST NJT Racing) and Chloe Jones (Monster Energy Crescent Yamaha) at 19 and 28 points respectively behind Ponziani. The Thai rookie arrives in Jerez having added two podiums to her tally from the last three races, but she also suffered her first DNF on Sunday at Donington Park. Another hurdle for her will be that she has never raced at Jerez. It’s been a slower season for Jones compared to her 2025 debut, however she returned to the podium in Race 1 at Misano and will hope to do the same at Jerez. The fight from seventh to eleventh is led by Spanish rider Pakita Ruiz (PR46+1 Racing Team), who, with 73 points, will fight in her home round, hoping to match her season-best P5 and take a final podium to close the year. Yvonne Cerpa (MotosCerpa-Gradara Corse) is one point behind her compatriot, and after a very solid debut season, she will want to take one more step up onto the podium. Natalia Rivera (Terra & Vita GRT Yamaha WorldWCR Team) continues to make progress in her second WorldWCR campaign. She knows this circuit well; she took two top-ten finishes here in 2025. She trails Cerpa by eight points and leads Sara Sanchez (Hadden Racing Team) by five. The #64 has had an uphill 2026 season and hasn’t been able to show her typical high level, which will make her want to close the 2026 season on a high note that much more. Mexican rider Astrid Madrigal (Pons Italika Racing FIMLA) finds herself in 11th place, a single point behind the #64 and will look to snatch a top ten position from her. Joy Bruno will replace Karolina Danak with the Prata Motor Sport squad during the final round of the year. Meanwhile, French rider Carla Mulot will ride in the place of the injured Lucie Boudesseul with the GMT94 Yamaha outfit. Colombian rider Sara Varon and Avalon Lewis (Carl Cox Motorsports) return to the field at Jerez as the round's two wildcards, although the Kiwi will first need to pass a checkup at the medical centre. signals.title: BRAKING IN DETAIL: Brembo explain ‘highly demanding’ Jerez circuit
signals.summary: It’s an iconic venue for two-wheeled motorsport and Brembo have explained some of the braking forces required to master Jerez The MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship will take on the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia for the final round of the 2026 campaign this weekend. Brembo engineers have detailed how tough the Spanish venue is on brakes and provided information about the circuit from their perspective. With Brembo supplying brakes to 13 out of WorldSBK’s 14 teams, they provide a unique insight into WorldSBK and the end-of-season Pirelli Spanish Round. It’s perhaps no surprise, given some of its tight corners after high-speed sections, that Jerez is rated as highly demanding on the brakes by Brembo, giving it a 4 out of 5 in this metric. Riders are on the brakes 10 times across the 4.423km layout for just under 28 seconds. This equates to about 29% of a lap at Jerez. With 13 turns that wind their way through the Spanish countryside, get up to speed with the Jerez circuit Dani Pedrosa corner, Turn 6, is considered the most demanding turn as riders scrub off an enormous amount of speed: arriving at 282km/h, they drop down to 68km/h in under five seconds and covering more than 200 metres while braking. Riders are applying 5.5kg to the brake lever and deceleration reaches 1.5g, while Brembo brake fluid pressure reaches 11.7 bar. Jerez often provides close racing due to its varied layout: it has tight and twisty sections and high-speed runs followed by heavy braking. Sector 1 features Turns 1-4, with the opening corner a key overtaking hot spot. In Sector 2, it’s vital to get a good exit from Turn 5 as it leads down the back straight and into Turn 6 – a key action hotspot in every class. The third sector is generally more single file, although you do see moves into Turns 9 and 10 occasionally, and it’s important to exit Turn 10, Peluqui, well; from there, it’s all about building speed to Turn 13, Jorge Lorenzo corner, where races can be won and lost in an instant. For Iker Lecuona (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati), his favourite part of Jerez is Turn 6: “The section I like the most is Turn 6. The braking and then the corner itself. It has hard braking into a very tight right-hander, so it is a really good spot to make some overtakes. I felt some comfortable there during the last few years in this corner.”. 2026 WorldSSP Champion Albert Arenas (AS BLU CRU Racing Team) points out the bump on the entry to the corner, just before the braking point. For the #75, his favourite part of Jerez is Turns 8-10: I really love Sector 3, starting at Turn 8. On this exit, you are sliding on the bike and then changing direction into Turn 9. It is technical, but at the same time, it’s fun. You have to be so precise. If you nail it well, it is so satisfying. It is also an important section of the circuit.” Watch every moment LIVE and UNINTERRUPTED from Jerez using the WorldSBK VideoPass – now only €4.99!

signals.title: “After several years, we now close the circle in WorldSBK”
signals.summary: The last pre-round debriefs of the year are here and we’ve gathered the best quotes from Jerez for you The MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship has hit the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia for the final round of the 2026 campaign. It’s a weekend of goodbyes to some, potential farewells to others and a chance to end the year on a high for everyone in the Pirelli Spanish Round. Read the best from Thursday’s debriefs below. Previewing his final round in WorldSBK, Nicolo Bulega (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) said: “It’s very emotional as it’s my last weekend here with WorldSBK and with my team. I remember a lot of things over these years. The last round of the season is always special, but this year, it will be even more special. I had my first WorldSSP test here back in November 2021, after several years, we now close the circle here in WorldSBK. It’s been an amazing five years. It’s very emotional because I think about all the good things over the last five years with this team. Luckily, it’s been more nice moments than bad moments. There were very good years here in WorldSBK with this team. It will be the last race, but I will always stay in contact with this team, and I’ll be their biggest fan next year. Every year is different, honestly, I have a good feeling on this track: I won the WorldSSP title, I had my first Moto3 pole and podium here as well as winning WorldSBK races in 2024 and 2025. It’s a good track for Ducati, so, I hope to be fast this year too. My birthday is on Friday, the best gift for me will be to finish the season strong and fast this weekend.” The 2026 Champion walked through what's been an "emotional" couple of days and hopes to end on a high note at Jerez Alvaro Bautista (Barni Spark Racing Team) spoke about his home round, potentially his last in WorldSBK. He said: “It's been a really, really tough season for me, for my team, because we didn't achieve the target we wanted to. In fact, we weren’t close to the target. Jerez is a fantastic track, I love it. I raced here for many, many, many years. I’ve had good and bad results here, but I always try to keep only the positive. The last time I raced here, I had good memories because we did really well; it was a strong weekend. We've arrived here with the mentality to keep pushing and to keep working because our performance was good. If I can enjoy the bike as I did at Estoril, it would be nice to end the season with a podium. The front two are a bit far away from the rest, but the fight for the podium is always difficult because there are a lot of riders fighting for it. At the moment, all I have assured is this weekend, so I will try to enjoy it, and then I will see. After the race I would like to take some time to breathe and see which options I have for my future. It has to be something that motivates me to keep racing. At the moment I feel good physically and mentally. I still have performance, as we showed in Estoril and I think if I can get a good feeling with the bike, I can be fast and fight for top positions again.” Speaking about what could be his final round in WorldSBK, Danilo Petrucci (ROKiT BMW Motorrad WorldSBK Team) said: “I’m feeling good. I’m honestly happy to be here at Jerez, where we started our journey with BMW last November. It’s my last race with them, which isn’t very nice, but we have nothing to lose. We’ve done a reset and we’ll use the bike as it was in November. It’s my last round with BMW; I don’t know if it’s my last round in WorldSBK. As a factory rider, it will be. I don’t have a result in mind. This year’s been really tough. I had a lot of expectations, but it was difficult to reach those results. I just want to enjoy it. I don’t know what I’ll do next year. At the moment, everything is open. I still have a couple of opportunities to race in WorldSBK next year. I don’t know if it’s good or not. I have another opportunity in another championship, then I have many things to continue at home. I have a lot of pain in my body. I want to enjoy what I did in my career, and I think I need a bit of time to rest and understand which is the best option.” The three-time race winner has "a couple of options" to remain in WorldSBK, but is yet to decide on his 2027 plans Ahead of his home round, Iker Lecuona (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) stated: “I’m happy and excited to finish an amazing season for me and my team. I know it’ll be a hard weekend for me, because I always struggle a lot at Jerez and I’ve had a lot of injuries here. It’s similar to Australia. My first big crash was here at Turn 12. I hurt my arm, the collarbone, the vertebra… and I crashed there again in my first test in WorldSBK. I broke my hand. Not my fault and I crashed and broke my foot at Turn 6. I don’t want to say beating Bulega is impossible because nothing is impossible, but it will be even harder than Estoril. He loves it and goes very fast. I don’t like it so much. I think 2026 has been 9 out of 10 for me. I don’t want to put a 10 because of Australia and the crash at Donington, the races at Misano… we could’ve done better. I think 9 because I had almost no crashes, when I need to push, I know when and why, so I didn’t take the extra risk like before. I’ve learnt a lot.” Xavi Vierge (Pata Maxus Yamaha) has his final round in blue on home soil. He said: “I’m very excited as always, it’s a great pleasure to be able to finish the season at home. signals.title: SCHEDULE: Full official schedule for the Jerez’s grand finale to the 2026 season
signals.summary: It all comes down to this: all four classes return for the final weekend of the campaign The 2026 MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship season arrives to the season’s climactic final round at the beloved Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia. The Pirelli Spanish Round kicks off with Free Practice for WorldWCR starting at 09:15 (all times Local Time UTC +2), followed up by WorldSPB at 09:55, WorldSBK’s Free Practice 1 at 10:35, and WorldSSP at 11:35. Later in the day, WorldWCR returns to set their Saturday grid with their Tissot Superpole session at 13:30, same for WorldSPB at 14:10. WorldSBK will set off in their FP2 at 15:00, tailed by WorldSSP who will close the opening day with a Superpole session at 16:00. WorldSBK rides in their FP3 session bright and early at 09:35 on Saturday, and will return to the track at 11:15 for their Tissot Superpole session. From there on, Saturday opens up the throttle, and hosts four races in a row to close out the day. signals.title: PREVIEW: Three-way fight for third place as the sun sets on Jerez in 2026’s WorldSSP campaign
signals.summary: For the last time this season, WorldSSP will don their leathers and fight to settle each of the season’s final awards The FIM Supersport World Championship season prepares for its grand finale at the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia, with the final accolades up for grabs at the Pirelli Spanish Round. All three titles were wrapped up at Estoril, but razor-thin margins separate riders in the top ten positions, including the coveted third-place spot. Albert Arenas (AS BLU CRU Racing Team) locked down the 2026 Riders’ Championship in Race 1 at Estoril last round as well as closing out the Teams’ and Manufacturers’ titles for a Yamaha clean sweep. He finished ahead of Valentin Debise (EASTROC ZXMOTO Factory Evan Bros Racing), who clinched second place in the Riders’ title in his Chinese manufacturer’s first season in the class. Several accolades still remain up for grabs, however, including the Riders’ Championship bronze medal, which is shaping up to go down to the wire in Spain. Can Oncu (Pata Yamaha Ten Kate Racing) currently holds third place, five points ahead of Jaume Masia (Orelac Racing VerdNatura) and Jeremy Alcoba (Kawasaki WorldSSP Team). The Turkish rider had a chaotic weekend in Portugal, crashing out of the lead in Race 1 and finishing P21; then, in Race 2, the #61 rode like a man possessed to salvage a strong result in P4 . Rain or shine, he attacked into Turn 1 and managed a fourth place to snatch P3 in the standings. third-place position. He took third, then fourth here last season, so anticipate another hard-charging podium fight from the #61. The two Spaniards sit tied in fourth with 229 points. Alcoba arrives in better form than the other home rider, following his first career double at Cremona with a Race 1 P3 and a Race 2 win at Estoril, and he took second place in Jerez’s Race 1 last season. Masia will hope to put his recent form behind him as he hasn’t been on the podium in the last three rounds, and will anxiously hope he is ruled fit, as he was diagnosed with a partially fractured second metatarsal in his left foot. Working in the Valencian’s favour, he won the opening race here in 2025, creating a three-way battle for third that’s too close to call. Tom Booth-Amos (PTR Triumph Factory Racing) won the first race last round at Estoril before crashing out of Race 2 before the red-flag restart. While he is within 17 points of P3, making a bronze medal finish possible, the Pirelli Best Lap award is tied between the Brit and French rider Debise, with two races remaining, and will go down to the final race. 43 points behind the Brit in P7, Roberto Garcia (GMT94 Yamaha) will await the all-clear from the medical centre after Oncu hit his right leg in the run into Turn 1 at Estoril’s Race 2, where he was diagnosed with a sprain and a contusion on his knee. German Rider Philipp Oettl (Feel Racing WorldSSP Team) has seen his results trend to the latter half of the top ten as the 2026 season has continued, but he’s been consistent as ever, rarely missing the top 10, and a P6 finish at Estoril might pique his appetite at Jerez – where he has earned two podiums back in 2020 and 2021, both on Kawasaki machinery – as he sits just five points behind Garcia. In P9, Matteo Ferrari (WRP Racing) enjoyed podium finishes at Jerez in MotoE back in 2022 and 2020; he leads Lucas Mahias (GMT94 Yamaha), who occupies the final position in the top ten. Mahias found another gear at Estoril, starting from P2 in Race 1, and took back-to-back fifth-place finishes despite leading stretches of both races. Mahias is just one point ahead of Ferrari’s countryman Alessandro Zaccone (Ecosantagata Althea Racing Team), who celebrated a MotoE podium of his own here back in 2021. Zaccone sits 3 ahead of WorldSSP sophomore Aldi Mahendra (AS BLU CRU Racing Team), who fought for the podium at Estoril before he crashed from P2 two laps prior to the chequered flag. It will be Mahendra’s first time racing at WorldSSP as he missed last season's round at Jerez with injury. Further down the order, French rider Corentin Perolari (Honda Racing World Supersport) looks to lock up the WorldSSP Challenge award, and he will do so if he can outscore Raffaele De Rosa (QJMOTOR Factory Racing) by a single point in Race 1 and lose at most four points to any other challenge rider. If De Rosa starts both races, he will become the first rider to ever ride in 200 WorldSSP races. After making his 2026 debut at Magny-Cours this season, Spanish rider Jorge Navarro (PTR Triumph Factory Racing) will ride again in WorldSSP at home as he replaces Oli Bayliss. He took P7 in Race 1, so look for him to fight for a top-ten finish again. Despite crashing out of both races, Eric Fernandez (Cerba Yamaha Racing Team) impressed with his speed in his WorldSSP debut at Estoril. The Spanish rider led Race 1 before crashing and will look to raise eyebrows again at home as he returns for his second round. Fellow Spanish rider Hector Garzo (Renzi Corse) was ruled unfit at Estoril from a functional impairment he suffered with his left wrist contusion; he’ll look to get back to competing at home in Estoril if he is ruled fit. signals.title: PREVIEW: Bulega and Pirelli prepare for WorldSBK farewells as Jerez hosts the 2026 finale
signals.summary: Jerez will be an emotional round for so many reasons as a historic 2026 campaign comes to a close in the south of Spain The MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship’s 2026 season finale is here. The Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia hosts this year’s action as the campaign draws to a close, and it’s sure to be a dramatic round. There will be emotional farewells at the Pirelli Spanish Round while everyone on the grid will look to end what has been a record-breaking year of World Superbike action. World Superbike has exclusively used Pirelli tyres since 2004, but they will depart the paddock at the end of this season. They’ve helped propel 12 different riders to WorldSBK titles over the last 23 seasons, where records have been smashed and eras have been defined: from close title races, Jonathan Rea winning six consecutive Championships for Kawasaki between 2015 and 2020, there was the ‘Titanic Trio’ era and, of course, 2026 which has been historic for so many reasons. It’s one last round for Pirelli in WorldSBK at Jerez. Round 12 of 2026 is here as World Superbike hits Jerez for the final round of the year Nicolo Bulega (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) has already been crowned Champion and has broken so many records. He could add to that tally this weekend with an 11 th pole of the year, tying the best for a season tally with Ben Spies, while he could also make it 36 podiums. The record for rostrums in one campaign is 34, set in 2019, by Jonathan Rea. Of course, ‘Bulegas’ will say goodbye to WorldSBK after Jerez as he prepares to take on the MotoGP paddock. A few riders will also say farewell to their current outfit. Xavi Vierge (Pata Maxus Yamaha) will have one last round in Yamaha blue before he moves to Barni Ducati, replacing Alvaro Bautista (Barni Spark Racing Team), whose future is up in the air, with Bautista stating that he isn’t worried about what’s to come . Jerez is a circuit the #19 adores and he showed podium pace at Estoril, so could there be a fairytale ending to the two-time WorldSBK Champion’s stint with Barni Ducati? Elsewhere, Danilo Petrucci's (ROKiT BMW Motorrad WorldSBK Team) one season with BMW comes to an end at Jerez and the #9 will also be aiming to go out on a high after what’s been a tough year for the three-time race winner. Like Bautista, his future is unknown, but he has stated he has to decide whether to continue in WorldSBK . After his treble at Cremona, Iker Lecuona (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) would have wanted more from Estoril but he was beaten by Bulega all weekend. The #7 will look to end his debut Ducati campaign with more silverware but he’s stated in the past Jerez isn’t a circuit that suits him. The battle for bronze has simmered down a bit after Estoril. Yari Montella (Barni Spark Racing Team) holds a 53-point lead over Alex Lowes (bimota by Kawasaki Racing Team) so the #5 could cement his position in third place in Race 1, providing he remains 38 points or more clear of the #22. In his rookie campaign, Montella had a best of P11 at the Spanish venue, while Alex Lowes has taken a podium at Jerez before and hasn’t been out of the top six since 2023. While the Bimota rider will do everything he can to snatch third from Montella, he’ll also have to watch out for twin brother Sam Lowes (ELF Marc VDS Racing Team). The #14 sits just 12 points behind his sibling and will hope to bounce back from a disappointing Estoril to secure P4 in the standings; he can’t leapfrog Montella to take third. Lorenzo Baldassarri (Team GoEleven) is on course for his best WorldSBK finish as he sits sixth and his future is secure after renewing his contract with GoEleven Ducati. He’s six points ahead of Axel Bassani (bimota by Kawasaki Racing Team) after the #47 finished P7, P6 and P5 at Estoril. Both will be searching for their first Jerez rostrum. They could face competition from Alberto Surra (Motocorsa Racing). The rookie has been in sensational form in recent rounds, taking four podiums from Cremona and Estoril, including in all three races at the Portuguese venue. His recent results – only outside the top ten in Aragon Race 1, when he had a back of the grid penalty and when he crashed from P3 in Race 1 at Cremona – have seen him climb the standings and into eighth. He’s 35 points behind ‘Balda’, and 29 behind ‘El Bocia’ with 62 available at Jerez, so perhaps P6 and P7 in the World Championship is just a bit out of reach for the #67. He’s ahead of Bautista, who will look to cement his place in the top ten but watch out for Miguel Oliveira (ROKiT BMW Motorrad WorldSBK Team). The #88 found form at Estoril and is just one point behind the #19, so perhaps a late charge into the top ten isn’t off the cards. Tommy Bridewell (Superbike Advocates) will hope to consolidate 15 th in the standings ahead of Remy Gardner (GYTR GRT Yamaha WorldSBK Team) and Petrucci, while the Australian’s teammate, Stefano Manzi , will harbour hopes of overhauling his 15-point deficit to ‘Petrux’. Similarly, his Honda teammate, Somkiat Chantra , has taken four point-scoring finishes from the last six races. signals.title: Pirelli unveil Jerez tyre solutions ahead of their final WorldSBK round
signals.summary: The Italian company will bid farewell to World Superbike after Jerez, bringing an end to a partnership spanning more than two decades The MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship will take on the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia for the final round of the 2026 campaign. The Pirelli Spanish Round will be a farewell to Pirelli as the Official Tyre Supplier to WorldSBK since 2004 leave at the end of the season, but, ahead of their final weekend, they have unveiled their allocation for the 2026 season finale. For the rear tyres in World Superbike, Pirelli have opted to go for the softest possible tyres, with every option coming from the standard range. Available throughout the weekend will be the SC0 soft, which is the hardest of the available tyres, and the SCX supersoft, used often throughout the season – including last weekend at Estoril. The SCQ extrasoft is also in the allocation, although its use is limited to practice sessions, Tissot Superpole and the Tissot Superpole Race. Should it rain, riders can use standard Intermedia and standard SCR1 Rain tyres. Like the rear tyre allocation, the options at the front all come from the standard range. The SC1 soft is the softest of the two available to the field, and it is joined by the SC2 medium. The SC1 is used commonly throughout the season. Should it rain, riders can fit either the standard Intermediate or standard SCR1 Rain tyre to their bike. For the World Supersport field, like for WorldSBK, all the tyres come from the standard range. At the rear, riders can fit either the SC0 soft or the SCX supersoft to their machines. At the front, the choices are the SC1 soft or the SC2 medium. In the event of rain, only the standard SCR1 Rain tyre is available. On the allocation and Pirelli’s final round, Giorgio Barbier, Motorcycle Racing Director at Pirelli said: “The Pirelli Spanish Round will mark the final chapter in the long journey that began in 2004, when Pirelli joined World Superbike as Official Tyre Supplier. Over the years, we have built a partnership that has seen us become not just a supplier, but an active and strategic partner, contributing to the growth and development of the Championship. “Before saying our final goodbyes, however, we still have one last round ahead of us, which we want to approach with the same determination and the aim of bringing a particularly positive season to the best possible conclusion. The results achieved, with new records set at virtually every circuit and in a wide variety of conditions, have gone hand in hand with intensive development work, carried out alongside the teams right up to the final race. For this last event, we have chosen to retain the softest rear options, the extrasoft SCQ and supersoft SCX, which have been used throughout much of the season. The extensive data collected over the years at Jerez, both during races and in testing, confirms that these are the most effective options for tackling a circuit characterised by low-abrasion asphalt.” Follow the final round of the 2026 campaign in style using the WorldSBK VideoPass – now only €4.99!

signals.title: FORM GUIDE: Bulega aims to bow out of WorldSBK with more records
signals.summary: The #11 has already taken a heap of records this season and will look for more ahead of his MotoGP move The MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship heads to the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia for the final round of an historic season. Nicolo Bulega (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) has taken countless records this year and he could take more during the Pirelli Spanish Round before his move to MotoGP. Get up to speed with the stats and facts you need ahead of this weekend’s season finale. 2003 – Ducati won every race in the 2003 campaign (24), with the Bologna-based manufacturer aiming to repeat that in 2026 with 36 victories. 49/52 – Bulega currently sits on 49 wins. If he takes a hat-trick at Jerez, he will be on 52, level with Troy Bayliss in fifth place in the all-time list. 46 – Bulega is on a run of 46 podiums in WorldSBK, the longest streak of all time. He could reach 49 with three more at Jerez, putting him one shy of double the previous record (25, set by both Colin Edwards and Toprak Razgatlioglu). 37 – Ducati’s streak of 37 victories, which started in Race 1 at Estoril last season, is an all-time record. 33/34 – With one more podium in 2026, Bulega will match Rea for rostrums in one campaign. Rea claimed 34 in his 2019 title-winning year. 32 – Ducati are the manufacturer with the most podiums at Jerez, with 32. Kawasaki are second with 18. 21 – In 30 races at Jerez, 21 riders have taken a podium. 17-12 – Ducati are the most successful manufacturer with 17 wins, more than the sum of their competitors, Aprilia and Kawasaki (4 each), Yamaha (3), BMW (1). 17 – The last 17 wins here (starting from 2019) came only from the first two grid spots. 12 – Bulega’s treble at Estoril means he now holds the record for most WorldSBK hat-tricks. 10/11 – Bulega has the chance to match Ben Spies’ 2009 pole tally of 11 if he gets pole at Jerez. The Italian and the American will be tied for most poles in a single season. Ducati have a chance to claim every pole this season, a feat they recorded in 1992 (with 13 poles). 10 – Jerez so far has had 10 different polesitters; only two riders were able to record two pole positions here: Tom Sykes (2015, 2016), Nicolò Bulega (2024, 2025). 10-12 – In 2024, Toprak Razgatlioglu became the first rider with 10 podiums here, taking the record of 9 from Jonathan Rea. Last year, he increased his record to 12. 9 – Only one win here didn’t come from the first six grid places: that was Jonathan Rea, winning from 9 th in 2017, Race 2. 5-5 – The record number of wins here, 5, is split by Alvaro Bautista (Barni Spark Racing Team) and Bulega: they both claimed them with the Panigale V4R. 5 – The best winning streak for a manufacturer at this track belongs to Ducati: 5 from 2023 Race 1 to 2024’s Superpole Race; it was broken by BMW, winning Race 2 with Razgatlioglu. signals.title: ANDALUSIA ON TWO WHEELS: Discover a land made for exploring by motorcycle
signals.summary: Andalusia offers much more than just the racetrack: roads, landscapes, gastronomy, and immense cultural variety makes the region an ideal destination to explore on two wheels The roar of motorcycles will once again be heard at the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto in Andalusia with the arrival of the MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship, but the passion for two-wheeled travel doesn’t end when the chequered flag falls. Andalusia offers a prime setting to extend the experience beyond the track and discover a region that seems tailor-made for motorcycle riding. From roads winding through mountain ranges to costal landscapes, forests and desert areas, every route offers a unique way to explore the south of the Iberian Peninsula. One of the great appeals of motorcycle travel is that the journey itself is part of the experience, and Andalusia offers a vast array of places waiting to be discovered. Its heritage reflects the passage of numerous civilisations, whose influence is clear in the architecture, agriculture, cuisine, landscapes and even the character of its people. From the largest cities to the smallest villages, every stop offers a chance to discover a different part of the region’s history and culture. All of this is complemented by amenities designed to make the journey more than just a series of miles covered. Dining, accommodation and services accompany roads and trails that often traverse areas far removed from major population centres. The concept is simple: travel at a leisurely pace, pause, and turn every leg of the trip into an essential part of the experience. It is practically impossible to speak of a single Andalusian landscape. Its vastness and diversity make the region feel like a small continent. The Guadalquivir basin encompasses fertile rival plains, rolling farmlands and marshes stretching towards the coast, while the mountainous areas conceal forests and ravines that vary strikingly from one another. Further east, areas such as Tabernas, Guadix and the Granada Highlands emerge, featuring some of the continent’s most arid landscapes, while the Sierra Morena range presents a completely different facet of the region. This variety turns every day on the motorcycle into a unique experience. A single route might transition from wide-open roads to mountain stretches, rural areas or near-desert landscapes. Added to this is a climate, with mild winters, lush springs, sunny summers and colourful autumns, that makes a motorcycle getaway a viable option at almost any time of year. Andalusia also stands out for the richness of its natural and cultural heritage. The region boasts nine Biosphere Reserves and three National Parks, as well as over 120 historic sites designated as Assets of Cultural Interest. The journey can also lead to places like Los Millares in Almeria – one of the major historical landmarks featured in Andalusia’s cultural offerings. The list continues with elements that showcase the region’s immense diversity: over 64 million olive trees create a unique, human-shaped landscape, while the Pulpi Geode offers a completely different point of interest. For motorcyclists, this variety means that every stop can completely transform the character of the journey. Travelling through Andalusia also means discovering it through its gastronomy. The journey allows you to combine roads and landscapes with numerous stops to experience local products and traditions firsthand. Highlights, among other accolades, include the World Cheese Award won by Olavidia cheese and the international recognition received by baker Domi Velez; these are prime examples of a culinary culture that is an integral part of the experience. Motorcycle touring offers a way to experience this heritage from a different perspective: travelling at a pace that encourages stops, interactions with local communities, and the discovery of places often left off the beaten path. Moreover, this style of travel can be pursued sustainably, minimising environmental impact while contributing to community development and the preservation of local traditions. The possibilities are not limited to the tarmac, either. Andalusia offers routes along both roads and dirt tracks, ranging from long-distance journeys to shorter trips, that are also suitable for electric motorcycles. Many of these routes avoid highways and major urban centres, bringing travellers closer to a quieter, lesser-known side of Andalusia. The philosophy is to enjoy the ride at a leisurely pace: stopping to admire the scenery, discovering the local heritage and savouring the regional cuisine. With the arrival of WorldSBK at Jerez, the Pirelli Spanish Round serves as the perfect starting point to explore everything Andalusia has to offer beyond the racetrack. It is a land to traverse, pause in, explore and, above all, enjoy on two wheels. signals.title: Jack Miller (Yamaha) stellt klar: «Dann stehen wir alle wie Idioten da!»
signals.summary: Jack Miller hat kein Verständnis dafür, wenn MotoGP-Fahrer Promotion-Aktivitäten schwänzen – niemand würde über den Regeln stehen. Andererseits fordert der Australier eine Bezahlung für den Aufwand. Die Neuausrichtung der MotoGP-WM unter Liberty Media ist deutlich zu spüren. Den Fans wird an den Wochenenden neben der Action auf der Rennstrecke immer noch mehr Unterhaltung geboten. Damit soll auch ein breiteres Publikum angesprochen werden – ganz im Sinne des Wachstums. Vor allem die Fahrer werden für die Vermarktung der Motorrad-Weltmeisterschaft herangezogen. Für die Stars der Show kommen an den ohnehin stressigen MotoGP-Wochenenden zusätzliche Verpflichtungen hinzu. Dies sorgte zuletzt vermehrt für Diskussionen. Beim Indonesien-GP wurde zudem eine Geldstrafe von 5.000 Euro für das Versäumen einer Promotion-Aktivität angekündigt. Pramac-Yamaha-Ass Jack Miller ist bekannt dafür, dass er sich kein Blatt vor den Mund nimmt. Auch zu diesem Thema hat «Jackass» eine klare Meinung. «Wenn es erwartet wird, dann muss man eben mitmachen. Ich finde nicht, dass man sich da herausnehmen soll», betonte der Australier. «Wir sitzen alle in einem Boot – was macht denn jemanden so besonders, dass er nicht teilnimmt, während der Rest von uns mitmacht? Wenn wir alle darauf verzichten, stehen wir wie Idioten da. Niemand steht über den Regeln.» Vor den Grands Prix haben die Fahrer in den jeweiligen Ländern oft Fan-Auftritte zu absolvieren. Dazu kommen Show-Events während der Rennwochenenden – so wie zuletzt das Go-Kart-Rennen in Japan. «Ich verstehe, dass es immer mehr wird, und irgendwann werden sie uns dafür auch bezahlen müssen – die Fahrer, meine ich», forderte Miller. «Denn wenn man immer mehr macht und das Geld, was reinkommt, immer weniger wird… so läuft das nun mal!» Noch ein Jahr Schule, dann Vollzeit-Profi! signals.title: Prestige-Duell in Portimão: Valentino Rossi tritt gegen Max Verstappen an
signals.summary: MotoGP-Ikone Valentino Rossi startet am kommenden Wochenende beim GT World Challenge Europe Endurance Cup in Portimão. Dort bekommt es der «Doktor» mit Formel-1-Ass Max Verstappen zu tun. Am kommenden Wochenende findet das Saisonfinale der weltgrössten GT3-Rennserie statt, des GT World Challenge Europe Endurance Cup. Gefahren wird auf der Berg- und Talbahn Autódromo Internacional do Algarve in Südportugal. Im Rahmen des Bahrain-GP in Malaysia hatte Formel-1-Champion Max Verstappen bestätigt, dass er in der Algarve antreten wird. In diesem Jahr absolvierte Verstappen bereits mehrere GT3-Einsätze auf der Nürburgring-Nordschleife und kämpfte beim 24h-Rennen bis zum Sonntagmittag um den Gesamtsieg, ehe er von einem Defekt eingebremst wurde. Einer von Max Verstappens Gegner in Portugal: Der neunfache Motorrad-Weltmeister Valentino Rossi, BMW-Werksfahrer seit 2023. Rossi sagt nun gegenüber der italienischen Sky: «Das wird fabelhaft, aber gleichzeitig wird Max Verstappen zu einem Riesen-Problem, weil der Kerl einfach so sauschnell ist.» «Ich hätte mir nie träumen lassen, dass ich eines Tages mal gegen Max Verstappen Rennen fahren werde. Es ist grossartig für alle, dass er in Portugal an den Start geht, und ich hoffe, ich kann mich an ihn dranhängen und von ihm so viel als möglich lernen.» Verstappen hat damit einen Lauf von sieben Rennwochenenden in Folge: Baku, Sepang und Singapur in der Formel 1, nun GT3, dann ebenfalls unmittelbar hintereinander Texas, Mexiko und Brasilien. Max freut sich ebenfalls: «Valentino ist eine coole Socke, und ich hoffe, wir können ein wenig Zeit zusammen verbringen. Im Rennen allerdings will ich ihn lieber nicht in meiner Nähe haben. Wenn’s nach mir geht, dann wünsche ich mir ein schönes, einsames Rennen an der Spitze.» «Aber ich weiss, die gut die Fahrer in dieser Serie sind, also mache ich mich da gefasst auf ganz viel Gegenwind.» «GT3 ist so ganz anders als Formel 1, aber ich liebe es. Ich bin auf der Nordschleife auf den Geschmack gekommen, und die Rennstrecke von Portimão ist herrlich. Ich will jede Runde geniessen. signals.title: Alex Rins (Yamaha) frustriert: «Ich bedauere das Motorrad, das wir haben»
signals.summary: Alex Rins beendete das MotoGP-Rennen am Sonntag in Indonesien auf dem enttäuschenden 15. Rang. Der Spanier war danach niedergeschlagen – welche Probleme er mit seiner Yamaha M1 hatte. Es wäre Alex Rins zu wünschen gewesen, dass er bei seinen letzten MotoGP-Rennen noch einige gute Resultate erzielen könnte. Doch die Yamaha M1 ist derzeit nicht konkurrenzfähig, was sich auch beim Großen Preis von Indonesien gezeigt hat. Im Sprint landete Rins direkt hinter seinem Teamkollegen Fabio Quartararo auf Rang 10, im Grand Prix wurde er nur 15. Insbesondere im Sonntagsrennen konnte Rins mit seinem Motorrad kein gutes Gefühl aufbauen – er hatte mit einigen Schwierigkeiten zu kämpfen, weshalb er beim anschließenden Medientermin immer noch frustriert war. «Was das Rennen angeht, hatte ich wirklich ein schlechtes Gefühl – nicht dasselbe wie am Freitag oder am Samstag», haderte der Spanier. «Die Strecke verändert sich und für jeden ändert sich alles. Bei meinem Bike war die Motorbremse inkonsistent, ebenso die Traktionskontrolle. Ab der ersten Runde war es während des gesamten Rennens ein wirklich schlechtes Gefühl. Dann waren auch noch die Reifen überhitzt – die gleiche Geschichte wie immer.» Im langen Rennen wollte Rins eigentlich den weichen Reifen verwenden. Doch sein Team hat ihm davon abgeraten, weshalb er diesen nicht verwendete. Bereut er diese Entscheidung? «Nein, ich bereue es nicht – wir sind ein Team», winkte er ab. «Was ich bedauere, ist das Motorrad, das wir haben.» In Indonesien hatten auch die Honda-Piloten ihre Schwierigkeiten, was die schlechten Ergebnisse belegen. Im Sprint war Johann Zarco als Zwölfter bester RC213V-Fahrer, im Grand Prix belegte Luca Marini als bester Honda-Pilot Platz 12. Vorne gaben Aprilia und Ducati den Ton. KTM konnte einigermaßen mithalten. Für die japanischen Hersteller Honda und Yamaha wäre es wichtig, insbesondere bei den Rennwochenenden in Asien, wo sich die Heim-Märkte befinden, konkurrenzfähig zu sein und gute Leistungen zu zeigen. «Wir haben seit Beginn an zu kämpfen – seit dem ersten Rennen. Es sieht so aus, als hätte Honda auf dieser Strecke mehr zu kämpfen gehabt als bei den anderen Rennen. Aber für uns ist es immer das Gleiche», stellte Alex Rins klar. signals.title: Trackhouse: Justin Marks verkauft Team-Anteile an britische Investoren
signals.summary: Justin Marks hat einen Teil seines MotoGP-Teams Trackhouse Racing an die britische Investitionsplattform «1936» verkauft. Welches Ziel hinter dem Deal steckt und was Liberty Media damit zu tun hat. Am 14. Oktober verkündete «1936» – laut eigener Angabe eine globale Investitionsplattform für Sport und Unterhaltung – von Justin Marks Anteile am Trackhouse-MotoGP-Team gekauft zu haben. Es soll sich um eine «bedeutende Minderheitsbeteiligung» handeln. Weitere finanzielle Details zu dem Deal wurden nicht bekanntgegeben. «Es ist ein aufregender Moment für das Superfile Trackhouse MotoGP Team, die Aufnahme von 1936 bekannt zu geben», sagte Teambesitzer Justin Marks am Mittwoch in einer offiziellen Aussendung von 1936. «Beide Gruppen sind fest davon überzeugt, dass die MotoGP-Weltmeisterschaft weltweit großes Potenzial birgt und dass Trackhouse bei diesem Wachstum eine herausragende Rolle spielen kann. Das Team hat nun zahlreiche Möglichkeiten, gemeinsam mit einer Gruppe vielfältiger und talentierter Partner erhebliche Investitionen in den Rennsport, die Marke, das Storytelling und das Trackhouse-Erlebnis zu tätigen.» Gründer und CEO der in London ansässigen Gruppe 1936 ist Charlie Raposo – ein ehemaliger britischer Skirennläufer. Laut 1936 würde die Investition zu einem entscheidenden Zeitpunkt für die MotoGP erfolgen. Durch die Übernahme von Liberty Media würde die internationale Fangemeinde wachsen und das Interesse seitens globaler Marken und Medienpartner zunehmen. «Gemeinsam wird die Eigentümergruppe bedeutende Investitionen in das Wachstum und den Erfolg des Superfile Trackhouse MotoGP Teams tätigen – sowohl auf der Rennstrecke als auch im kommerziellen Bereich –, während der Sport in eine neue Ära der globalen Expansion eintritt», hieß es seitens 1936. «Wir glauben, dass die MotoGP erst am Anfang ihrer kommerziellen Möglichkeiten steht», ergänzte Charlie Raposo. «Die Rennen gehören wohl zu den besten im Motorsport, und die wachsende Fangemeinde ist äußerst loyal und engagiert. Es ist bereits ein globaler Sport mit erheblichem Wachstumspotenzial auf internationaler Ebene. Justin hat ein Team mit echtem Ehrgeiz und eine Marke aufgebaut, die sich von anderen abhebt, und wir sind stolz darauf, ihn auf seinem Weg zu begleiten, das leistungsstärkste MotoGP-Team auf und abseits der Rennstrecke aufzubauen. Wir freuen uns darauf, gemeinsam mit dem Team das spannendste Franchise in diesem Sport zu entwickeln.» Sportlich läuft es für Trackhouse Aprilia in der MotoGP-Saison 2026 sehr gut. Ai Ogura und Raul Fernandez belegen derzeit in der Fahrerwertung die Ränge 4 und 7. signals.title: Sind die 850er-Bikes zu schnell? Dall’Igna und Rivola nahmen Stellung dazu
signals.summary: Bei den privaten Tests für die neue MotoGP-Ära ab 2027 zeigt sich, dass die 850er-Prototypen mit den Pirelli-Reifen nicht viel langsamer sind als die 1000er-Bikes. Was Ducati und Aprilia dazu sagen. 2027 treten in der MotoGP die neuen Regeln in Kraft. Diese schreiben eine Hubraumreduzierung von 1000 auf 850 ccm, den Wegfall der Systeme zur Fahrwerkshöhenverstellung (Devices) und eine reduzierte Aerodynamik vor. Dazu kommt bei den Reifen der Wechsel von Michelin auf Pirelli. Ziel der Maßnahmen ist es, die Geschwindigkeit in der Königsklasse der Motorrad-WM zu reduzieren. Die fünf Hersteller – Ducati, Aprilia, KTM, Honda und Yamaha – arbeiten intensiv an den neuen Motorrädern für die nächste Saison. So wurden in diesem Jahr bereits viele Testkilometer absolviert. Bei den privaten Tests wurden bislang zwar keine offiziellen Zeiten bekanntgegeben, es ist jedoch längst durchgedrungen, dass die 850er-Bikes mit den Pirelli-Reifen alles andere als langsam sind. Wie SPEEDWEEK.com berichtete , fuhr LCR-Honda-Rookie Diogo Moreira beim Spielberg-Test die schnellste Zeit. Die Rundenzeit des Brasilianers lag bei 1:28,4 min. Zum Vergleich: Im Qualifying am Rennwochenende schaffte Moreira mit der 1000er-Honda eine Zeit von 1:29,1 min. Ein weiteres Beispiel: Die Zeit von Pedro Acosta auf dem Red Bull Ring, die beim Grand Prix für die erste Startreihe gereicht hat, lag bei 1:27,9 min. Der KTM-Pilot fuhr dann beim Test mit der 850er eine 1:28,9 min. Die neuen Regeln 2027 sollen die MotoGP-Bikes eigentlich einbremsen. Wie es aussieht, sind die Rundenzeiten der 850er-Motorräder mit den Pirelli-Reifen jetzt schon nah dran an den 1000ern mit den Michelin-Gummis. Ducati-Corse-CEO Gigi Dall’Igna und Aprilia-Rennchef Massimo Rivola nahmen beim Indonesien-GP Stellung zu diesem Thema. «Der Hauptgrund, warum wir die Leistung reduzieren möchten, ist nicht die Leistung an sich – es ist die Geschwindigkeit, mit der die Fahrer in der Kurve ankommen», entgegnete Gigi Dall’Igna. «Aus diesem Grund reduzieren wir die Motorleistung und den Hubraum. Selbst wenn die Rundenzeiten ziemlich nah an denen von 2026 liegen, können wir dadurch an Sicherheit gewinnen. Ehrlich gesagt, halte ich dies für einen Schritt, den wir machen müssen.» Apropos Top-Speed: Jorge Martin und sein Aprilia-Teamkollege Marco Bezzecchi stellten beide im Mai in Mugello mit 368,6 km/h einen MotoGP-Geschwindigkeitsrekord auf. «In Mugello fuhren sowohl Marco als auch Jorge 368,6 km/h, und das ist schnell», sagte Massimo Rivola. «Wenn man also mehr oder weniger 50 Pferdestärken wegnimmt, wird das diesen Speed sicherlich verringern. Nach dem, was wir sehen, scheinen die Rundenzeiten immer noch recht schnell zu sein. Gleichzeitig sagen die Fahrer, dass sich das Motorrad leichter fahren lässt. Vielleicht lässt es sich also etwas besser handhaben. Aber es ist besser, nach vorne zu schauen als zurück, da es beschlossen ist.» Rivola gab zudem zu Bedenken, dass das Bild in den Rennen ein anderes sein könnte. «Wir wissen nicht, ob die Zeiten über die gesamte Renndistanz hinweg gleich schnell ist», so der Italiener. «Auf eine einzelne Runde scheinen die Motorräder recht schnell zu sein – auf manchen Strecken vielleicht sogar sehr schnell, mit einem geringen Zeitabstand im Vergleich zu den 1000ern. Aber ganz sicher ist der Reifen der entscheidende Faktor, der momentan noch eine Unbekannte ist.» Noch ein Jahr Schule, dann Vollzeit-Profi! Bezzecchi und Aprilia feiern historischen Sieg Startcrash! signals.title: Estoril 2006: Als zwei Außenseiter Valentino Rossi die Show stahlen
signals.summary: Beim vorletzten Rennen der Saison 2006 fuhren mit Toni Elias und Kenny Roberts jr. zwei Underdogs um den Sieg. P1 wurde entschieden im engsten Fotofinish der MotoGP-Ära. Es kostete Rossi den WM-Titel. Der 15. Oktober 2006 in Estoril hätte ein Rossi-Fest werden sollen. Stattdessen lieferte das vorletzte Saisonevent eines der besten Rennen der MotoGP-Geschichte, in welchem zwei Piloten an der Spitze mitfuhren, mit denen kaum jemand gerechnet hatte: Der spanische Gresini-Pilot Toni Elias und der Privatier Kenny Roberts jr. Nachdem ein Zwischenfall in der fünften Runde die WM durcheinandergewirbelt hatte – Doppelausfall der Repsol-Honda-Piloten Nicky Hayden und Dani Pedrosa –, führte zunächst Valentino Rossi vor seinem Yamaha-Kollegen Colin Edwards. Dahinter formierte sich eine Spitzengruppe. Elias, von Startplatz 11 gekommen, arbeitete sich nach vorn, Roberts jr. pflügte von Rang 13 durchs Feld. Aus dem vermeintlichen Rossi-Spaziergang wurde ein Vierkampf. Dass gleich zwei Außenseiter um den Sieg kämpften, war 2006 zwar selten, aber möglich. Honda verteilte seine RC211V großzügig: Neben dem Werksteam Repsol erhielten Kundenteams wie Fortuna Gresini nahezu gleichwertiges Material. Roberts jr. wiederum fuhr mit der KR211V ein selbst gebautes Chassis mit Honda-Motor. Es war der letzte von einem Privatteam konstruierte Prototyp, der je ein MotoGP-Rennen anführte und auf dem Podest stand. In den Jahren danach kippte dieses Gleichgewicht. Mit der 800er-Ära verkamen Satelliten-Bikes zu Vorjahresmaschinen, echte Außenseitersiege verschwanden – bis Jack Miller 2016 in Assen gewann. Heute sind die Karten wieder anders gemischt: In der Gegenwart erhalten unabhängige Teams beinahe aktuelles Material. 2024 wurde Jorge Martin auf der Pramac-Ducati als erster Privatfahrer MotoGP-Weltmeister. Das Finale in Estoril war Racing in höchster Form. In der letzten Runde wechselte die Führung mehrfach, Rossi zog in der letzten Kurve noch einmal vorbei – doch Elias klebte im Windschatten und schob sich auf der Ziellinie vor den Doktor. Zwei Tausendstelsekunden – es ist bis heute das engste Fotofinish der MotoGP-Ära. Roberts jr. wurde Dritter, es war das 22. und letzte GP-Podest seiner Laufbahn. Für Elias blieb es der einzige Sieg in der Königsklasse, und für Rossi hatte der zweite Platz einen bitteren Preis: Die fünf Punkte, die er in Estoril liegen ließ, sollten exakt jene fünf sein, die ihm am Saisonende zum Titel fehlen würden. In der Saison 2006 wurde in Valencia mit Nicky Hayden der letzte MotoGP-Weltmeister aus den USA gefeiert. Noch ein Jahr Schule, dann Vollzeit-Profi! signals.title: WM-Leader Jorge Martin (Aprilia): Infusion nach Magen-Darm-Infektion
signals.summary: Aprilia-Ass Jorge Martin schont sich auch in der kurzen MotoGP-Auszeit nicht. In Asien fing er sich zudem eine Magen-Darm-Infektion ein. Der «Martinator» musste am Mittwoch ärztlich behandelt werden. Nach dem Indonesien-GP befindet sich die MotoGP derzeit in einer kurzen Auszeit – bevor mit Australien, Malaysia und Katar drei Rennwochenenden direkt nacheinander folgen. Einige Protagonisten der Königsklasse sind nach dem heißen Mandalika-Event sofort wieder zurück nach Europa gereist. Andere MotoGP-Asse wiederum nutzen das kommende freie Wochenende für einen verlängerten Aufenthalt in Asien. Dazu gehört auch WM-Leader Jorge Martin, der sich vor der beschwerlichen Anreise zum Australien-GP kein weiteres Mal dem Jetlag aussetzen wollte. Der Spanier ist mit seiner Freundin Maria in Indonesien geblieben, er kombiniert dort Erholung mit Trainingssessions. Am Mittwoch sorgte der 28-jährige Aprilia-Pilot für Aufsehen, als er auf Social Media ein Bild von sich mit einer Infusion zeigte und dazu kurz und knapp meinte, es gäbe «Probleme». Was war passiert? Der Spanier hat sich eine Magen-Darm-Infektion eingefangen, dies wurde von Aprilia-Verantwortlichen gegenüber SPEEDWEEK.com auch bestätigt. Deswegen bekam der «Martinator» am Mittwochabend in seinem privaten Appartement Besuch von einem Arzt, der ihn mit einer Vitamin-Infusion versorgte. Fakt ist: Martin schont sich kaum, trainiert auch an den freien Tagen so gut wie täglich – ob mit Einheiten auf dem Rennrad oder im Fitnesscenter. Bei Aprilia will man den Weltmeister von 2024 auch gar nicht groß einbremsen. Martin hat Erfahrung mit engen WM-Fights, er hat bereits 2024 im Duell gegen Pecco Bagnaia in den Übersee-Runden den Grundstein für den Triumph zu seinen Gunsten gelegt. signals.title: Dall’Igna über den Indonesien-GP: «Haben den Schaden in Grenzen gehalten!»
signals.summary: Ducati rechnete beim MotoGP-Event in Indonesien mit einer Klatsche. Dank Champion Marquez und Patzern von Aprilia lief es besser als erwartet. Mastermind Gigi Dall’Igna lobte «Marcs Genialität». Was den Titelkampf in der MotoGP angeht, kann Marc Marquez zufrieden sein mit seinem Auftritt in Indonesien. Im Sprint siegte er, den Grand Prix beendete der 33-Jährige auf Rang 6 – er sah dort das erste Mal in einem Sonntagsrennen die Zielflagge. Vor dem Event auf dem Mandalika International Street Circuit stand bereits fest, dass es für Ducati ein schwieriges Rennwochenende werden wird – das haben die Ergebnisse aus der Vergangenheit gezeigt. Rivale Aprilia hingegen war als haushoher Favorit angetreten. Die Dinge nahmen ihren Lauf. Am Samstag stand sich der Hersteller aus Noale selbst im Weg. Marco Bezzecchi und Raul Fernandez beförderten sich gegenseitig ins Aus und Jorge Martin musste sich in Führung liegend zurückfallen lassen – Schuld war wieder einmal ein zu geringer Druck im Vorderreifen. Am Sonntag lief dann alles glatt für die RS-GP-Piloten: Es wurde ein Vierfachsieg, zudem konnte Martin die WM-Führung zurückerobern. Dennoch ging MM93 als Sieger aus dem Event hervor – er schaffte in Indonesien mehr, als er und auch die Roten erwartet haben. «Es war ganz klar kein einfaches Wochenende für uns, und dennoch war es meiner Meinung nach ein positives», unterstrich Ducati-Corse-CEO Gigi Dall’Igna in seiner Analyse auf LinkedIn. «Es bringt neue Energie – natürlich nicht die eines Sieges, sondern die Art von Energie, die daraus entsteht, dass wir Chancen nutzen, die Zähne zusammenbeißen und wertvolle Punkte holen, auch wenn wir in der Defensive sind. Genau das war bei unserem Sprint-Sieg und dem sechsten Platz im langen Rennen am Sonntag der Fall. Auch wenn Letzteres als bescheidenes Ergebnis erscheinen mag, ermöglicht es uns in Kombination mit dem Sieg am Samstag, von dort abzureisen, ohne dass sich unser Rückstand in der Meisterschaft verändert hat. Wir haben den Schaden mit purem Können und Erfahrung auf einer Strecke begrenzt, von der wir wussten, dass sie hart sein würde – vielleicht unsere schwierigste und definitiv eine, die unseren Gegnern zugutekam. Tatsächlich hatte es Marc auf dieser Strecke zuvor noch nie geschafft, in einem Sonntagsrennen die Ziellinie zu überqueren.» Dall’Igna lobte die Leistung von Marc Marquez in höchsten Tönen: «An diesem Wochenende zeigte sich so viel von Marcs Genialität: Bereit zu sein, wenn es am wichtigsten ist, um einen unerwarteten ersten Platz zu ergattern, und den Scharfsinn zu zeigen, kritische Momente zu meistern, wenn das Motorrad nicht das stärkste im Feld ist, und das absolute Maximum aus jeder Situation herauszuholen, selbst aus der ungünstigsten.» «Eine große Hürde liegt nun hinter uns, ohne dass wir Schaden genommen haben», führte Dall’Igna weiter aus. «Tatsächlich fühlen wir uns jetzt sogar stärker und besser vorbereitet. Dennoch war es insgesamt ein anspruchsvoller GP für Ducati, wie die Ergebnisse unserer anderen Fahrer bestätigen. Wir wussten von Anfang an, dass es am Sonntag hart werden würde und dass wir kämpfen müssten. Unser Tempo reichte nicht an die Besten heran, also mussten wir uns anpassen, ohne die Motivation zu verlieren, und das große Ganze im Blick behalten. Und genau das haben wir getan – mit Konzentration, Klarheit und jener gesunden Portion Demut, die einem immer guttut.» Marc Marquez reist nun mit zwei Punkten Rückstand auf WM-Leader Jorge Martin nach Australien. Auf Phillip Island findet vom 23. bis 25. Oktober das nächste Rennwochenende statt. Bei den letzten fünf Grands Prix wird sich der Titelkampf weiter zuspitzen. «Jedes einzelne Rennen ist nun entscheidend für den endgültigen Titelkampf. Das mag wie ein Klischee klingen, ist aber absolut wahr!», so Dall’Igna. «Noch nie war der Abstand in dieser Phase der Weltmeisterschaft so knapp: eine echte Show. Möge der Beste gewinnen – mit jener unverwechselbaren Sportlichkeit und Fairness, die unser wunderschöner Sport verdient. Auf geht’s, Ducati!» Noch ein Jahr Schule, dann Vollzeit-Profi! signals.summary: Fermin Aldeguer hatte sich bei einem Crash im MotoGP-Rennen in Indonesien einen Bruch in der rechten Hand zugezogen. Oktober zum vorerst letzten Mal auf Phillip Island über die Bühne geht, dabei sein wird können, ist derzeit ungewiss. So werden die nächsten Tage für den Spanier ein Wettlauf gegen die Zeit. Aldeguer ist in seiner zweiten MotoGP-Saison vom Verletzungspech verfolgt. Anfang Januar hatte er auf dem Aspar Circuit nahe Valencia einen schweren Trainingssturz. signals.title: Nachricht von Valentino Rossi an Nicolo Bulega: An kommende Aufgaben denken
signals.summary: Superbike-Weltmeister Nicolo Bulega hat in dieser Saison reihenweise Rekorde niedergerissen. Dem Italiener ist bewusst, dass es so in der MotoGP nicht weitergeht – wie er sich darauf vorbereitet. Obwohl in der Superbike-WM noch drei Läufe in Jerez zu fahren sind, hat Champion Nicolo Bulega bereits jetzt eine Reihe der wichtigsten Rekorde auf der Habenseite. Er gewann 29 Rennen in einer Saison, der alte Rekord von Alvaro Bautista aus dem Jahr 2023 stand bei 27. Bulega triumphierte in neun der bislang elf Events in allen drei Läufen und hat mit 664 Punkten ebenfalls eine Bestmarke aufgestellt. Saisonübergreifend 44 Podestplätze in Folge gelangen vor ihm keinem, bezüglich Podestplätze in einer Saison (33) liegt nur noch Jonathan Rea vor ihm – der Nordire schaffte 2019 erstaunliche 34. Für 2027 und 2028 hat Bulega einen MotoGP-Vertrag mit dem VR46-Ducati-Team von Valentino Rossi unterschrieben und wird sich die Box mit dem talentierten Fermin Aldeguer teilen. Dann beginnt für ihn ein neuer Karriereabschnitt. «Wenn du nach dem Fahren zurück an die Box kommst und Platz 2 die schlechteste Position ist, dann kommst du mental in einen Bereich, der nicht real ist», schilderte Bulega beim Treffen mit SPEEDWEEK.com. «Schon gar nicht, wenn es um die MotoGP geht. Nächstes Jahr werde ich meinen Namen sicher nicht die ganze Zeit auf Platz 1 sehen. Ich werde mit einer anderen Einstellung in die Saison gehen. Das wird mein erstes Jahr in der MotoGP, ich muss vieles erst verstehen und der Level ist unglaublich hoch. Deshalb hege ich keine Erwartungen. So war es auch in meinem ersten Jahr in der Superbike-WM. Ich werde schuften, mein Maximum geben, den Fokus behalten, an Details hart arbeiten und versuchen, mit jedem Mal fahren näher an die Spitze zu kommen.» Nur wenige vorherige Superbike-Fahrer haben auch in der MotoGP Spitzenleistungen gebracht, zuletzt gelang das Cal Crutchlow. «Was Ben Spies gezeigt hat, war auch nicht so schlecht», meinte Bulega. «Er hatte dann aber Pech, ein paar Verletzungen. Wenn ein Fahrer stark ist, dann muss er versuchen, seinen Fahrstil an ein neues Motorrad anzupassen. Motorradrennen zu fahren ist ein schwieriger Sport: Du brauchst das richtige Bike und Team, musst selbst immer auf 100 Prozent sein und eine MotoGP-Saison ist sehr lang. Mal sehen, ob mir gute Resultate gelingen. Für mich wäre das schön, aber auch für das Superbike-Paddock.» Nach dem vorzeitigen Titelgewinn in Cremona am letzten September-Wochenende erhielt Bulega unzählige Gratulationen, auch über WhatsApp und Instagram: «Ich weiß es sehr zu schätzen, dass mir auch Rivalen gratuliert haben, auch einige MotoGP-Fahrer. signals.title: BMW’s highly-anticipated F450 RR supersport gets four variants
signals.summary: BMW reveals its all-new F450 RR supersport machine with four variants, all of which offer something a little bit different. Following the arrival of the naked F450 R in September, it was only a matter of time before Beemer expanded its new 450 range to include a fully-faired sibling. And that’s exactly what we have here with the A2 F450 RR, which is available in four different variants, including the Base model. Priced at £6,730, the standard model makes use of the same 420cc parallel-twin that’s housed by the £6,395 F450 R, and the F450 GS, which was the first model to arrive as part of BMW’s new 450 platform. That means riders are also getting the same 48hp (around 47bhp) at 8,750rpm and 31Ib-ft of torque at 6,750rpm as its naked and adventure siblings. This being said, the F450 RR is tuned for supersport use, meaning it features slightly different chassis geometry and ergonomics. The A2-compliant machine is also available in Sport (£6,875), M Sport (£6,995), and M Sport with Innovation Package (£7,250) variants. The Sport variant adds Shift Assistant Pro and the Sport suspension, while the M Sport includes both of those features, alongside Riding Modes Pro and the Snaefell white/M Motorsport colour scheme. Meanwhile, the Innovation Package adds Beemer’s Easy Ride Clutch system. Standard features aboard the new F450 RR include a two-piece seat with a height of 790mm, heated grips, LED lighting, a 6.5-inch TFT display, connectivity, and a USB-C port. Beemer also says the supersport machine features a fuel consumption of 3.8 liters per 100km (62 miles), while the 14-litre fuel tank provides a calculated range of more than 217 miles. Accessories such as a tank bag and soft cases can be added for riders that want to turn the F450 RR into more of a commuter. Suspension is handled by a 43mm KYB upside-down fork and a KYB rear shock, while the rear wheel is carried by an aluminium swingarm. With the Sport suspension up front, rebound and compression damping are adjustable. Stopping power comes via a 310mm front disc with a Brembo four-piston monobloc calliper at the front. A 240mm rear disc is mated to a floating ByBre single-piston caliper. The new BMW F450 RR also makes use of a welded tubular steel space frame featuring integrated forged components, while the parallel-twin engine is incorporated as a load-bearing element. Additionally, the bike rides on 17-inch wheels and has a ready-to-ride weight of 177kg. Markus Flasch, CEO BMW Motorrad, said this about the new F450 RR: “What I particularly like about the new BMW F 450 RR is how light, direct, and precise it is to ride. To me, that’s exactly what a supersport motorcycle should be. It’s great fun on twisty roads and performs just as well on the racetrack. At the same time, it clearly carries the DNA of our RR models. For me, it’s the perfect entry into the world of BMW RR motorcycles.” Find the latest motorcycle news on Visordown.com Stay up to speed with the latest motorcycling news and analysis, delivered straight to your inbox. signals.title: Ducati’s class-leading superbike gets even faster for 2027
signals.summary: Ducati has unleashed its new-for-2027 Panigale V4 and Panigale V4 S, which gain more power and electronics linked to its MotoGP bike. Ducati has unveiled its new Panigale V4 and V4 S models for 2027, with the latter now part of the Italian brand’s ‘Ducati Factory Made’ programme for the first time. What this means for customers interested in one of the 2027 V4 S models is that a whole plethora of colours are now available to choose from, including five taken directly from the Automobili Lamborghini Ad Personam catalogue. Customers can also take advantage of a range of homologated accessories that will be installed during the production phase. These include Front Brake PRO and PRO+ packages, an STM dry clutch, and adjustable footpegs. The V4 S version also benefits from new adjustable clip-on handlebars designed especially for track use. Ducati has raised them by 10mm to create a higher riding position, which follows the trend seen in MotoGP in recent years. This change should give riders better leverage on the handlebars, and therefore improved control and reduced physical effort during direction changes and under heavy braking. The V4 S has also gained numerous electronic changes for 2027, including Dynamic Engine Brake, which is a first for this particular model. The new system replaces the outgoing Engine Brake Control and uses the company’s DVO (Ducati Vehicle Observer) algorithm to modulate engine braking based on the actual load placed on the rear tyre. Additionally, the premium electronics package is further enhanced by the addition of the new Race Brake Control, which is derived from the most exclusive models in the Ducati range. Now, the new Panigale V4 is, at least in race trim, the class-leading superbike in the world at the moment. And based on the changes made for 2027, there’s a chance the standard model will continue to perform even better than before. That’s because the Panigale V4 posted an average lap time four tenths faster than the previous model during testing at the Vallelunga circuit in Italy. At the heart of the 2027 model is a refined 1,103cc Desmosedici Stradale engine that now produces 215bhp (two bhp more than before), thanks to modifications made to improve airflow and reduce mechanical friction. Ducati says “the greatest gains occur between 12,000 and 14,000rpm, including a peak increase of 3.5hp (3.4bhp) at 13,000rpm. Ducati has also adopted longer final gearing (17/42 instead of 16/41), which has helped the Panigale V4 increase its top speed by around 7.4mph). If customers want even more performance, a new Akrapovic Full Racing Exhaust PRO is also available, which adds 10.8bhp and 5Ib-ft of torque while reducing the bike's weight by 6.6kg. Finally, Ducati has also introduced a revised exhaust system, a new high-flow air intake (0.6 per cent more at roughly 186mph) and a recalibrated lubrication circuit to reduce power loss. The new Panigale V4 and Panigale V4 S will be available at European dealerships starting in March 2027, before North American dealerships receive the new models from April. Distribution will continue in other countries after that.
